llm: Claude Sonnet (one fresh agent, prompt = evidence sheet only, srlab.rag.prompt)
prompt:
You are helping a search-ranking engineer understand one failed search. Use ONLY the evidence sheet below. Every number you write must appear in the sheet exactly as written there. Cite retrieved cases as [1], [2], [3].

EVIDENCE SHEET

This search: member 304 asked "a fantasy film for grown-ups". The ranker put Aladdin (1992) first; the better match was Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002).
Why Aladdin (1992) (TemGX links, CATGX structure): 1 of 3 from other people's ratings, 2 of 3 from the title's recent raters; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Example links: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002) – user 297, rating 3.0 on 2015-12-08; Aladdin (1992) – user 425, rating 4.5 on 2015-12-27; Aladdin (1992) – user 533, rating 4.5 on 2016-04-04.
Why Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002): 1 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 2 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title.
Check by deletion: the graph model prefers Aladdin (1992) with 73% confidence; deleting Aladdin (1992)'s explanation links gives 46%; deleting Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002)'s gives 81%; deleting random links from the same period gives 72%.

Retrieved from 341 verified past diagnoses (most similar mechanism first):
  [1] member 246, "a comedy for grown-ups, not a kids movie": Hunt for Red October, The (1990) ranked above Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (2006). Why: 1 of 3 from other people's ratings, 1 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 1 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: understand what the request rules out.
  [2] member 142, "a musical, but not a romance": Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, The (2005) ranked above Robin Hood (1973). Why: 3 of 3 from the title's recent raters; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: understand what the request rules out.
  [3] member 508, "a mystery to watch tonight, nothing too dark": Great Escape, The (1963) ranked above Holes (2003). Why: 2 of 3 from the title's recent raters, 1 of 3 from the member's own ratings; structure: a taste path from the member to the title. Fixes that worked when re-ranked: none of the three.

Store recommendation: "understand what the request rules out" (worked for 18 of 20 most similar past failures). On held-out failures this kind of recommendation picked a working fix 39% of the time, vs 24% for always using "understand what the request rules out".

Write for a product manager, in plain everyday English: say 'ratings' (not links or edges), 'how sure the model is' (not confidence or probability), 'recent fans of the film' (not the title's recent raters); no jargon, no em dashes; short sentences.
Return JSON only, an object with keys:
  "diagnosis": one or two short sentences: what went wrong in this search and why;
  "precedent": one short sentence on what the similar past failures have in common with it, citing them;
  "recommendation": one short sentence on which fix to try and how far to trust it;
  "caveat": one short sentence on what this evidence does not show.

answer.diagnosis: The ranker put Aladdin (1992) first for "a fantasy film for grown-ups", but Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002) was the better match. The model was 73% sure of Aladdin. Its reasons came mostly from recent fans of the film (2 of 3), while Harry Potter's came mostly from the member's own ratings (2 of 3). Taking away Aladdin's ratings dropped how sure the model was to 46%, so those ratings drove the pick. Taking away random ratings from the same period barely moved it (72%).
answer.precedent: Like this search, past failures [1], [2] and [3] were all requests with a limit built in ("for grown-ups", "not a romance", "nothing too dark"), and a family-friendly film still won; in [2] and [3] recent fans of the film supplied most of the reasons, as here.
answer.recommendation: Try "understand what the request rules out", which worked for 18 of 20 of the most similar past failures, but trust it only moderately, since this kind of advice picked a working fix 39% of the time on new cases, against 24% for always using it.
answer.caveat: The evidence does not show that the fix will work for this search, because in [3] none of the three fixes worked, and it does not show why the ratings from recent fans pulled the model toward a kids' film.
